title: BAS: Bridging Adam and SignSGD for Memory-Efficient LLM Training
claim: One family of methods spans a spectrum between two extremes, and finer partitioning buys fidelity at the cost of more memory.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, bottom arrow labeled with the tradeoff axis
description: Three side-by-side neural-network diagrams show the same layered graph with different parameter groupings. The left panel, 'Signum Equivalence (Single Global Block)', colors every node and edge one muted khaki, so the whole network is one block. The middle panel, 'Block Adaptive Signum (BAS) (Variable Partitioning)', colors nodes and edges in a few groups (green, blue, brown, teal, pink), which marks the intermediate block structure. The right panel, 'Adam Equivalence (Element-wise Blocks)', gives every node and edge its own bright color, so each element is its own block. A thick black arrow runs left to right along the bottom, with the bold caption 'Increased granularity and memory overhead: O(#blocks)'. The eye goes first to the color contrast across the three panels.
caption: Schematic of the Block Adaptive Signum (BAS) spectrum. The algorithm partitions parameters x into disjoint blocks.
abstract: We propose Block Adaptive Signum (BAS) , which bridges Adam and SignSGD via block-wise scaling of sign updates. By discarding element-wise second moments, BAS reduces memory overhead relative to AdamW without sacrificing performance in our tested settings. Crucially, BAS mimics Adam’s dynamics closely enough to directly inherit its hyperparameters , matching the performance of AdamW without the need for re‑tuning, a common fragility of prior low‑memory optimizers. This structural alignment makes it particularly suitable for tuning Adam-pretrained models. Furthermore, we exploit the inherent robustness of sign-based updates to store the first moment in FP8 without performance degradation. This shrinks the optimizer‑state footprint to 12.5\% of AdamW’s . We theoretically prove convergence under standard assumptions and introduce a communication-efficient variant enabled by the sign-based update. Across extensive evaluations, including pre‑training a 1.5B model on 100B tokens and supervised fine-tuning of models up to 32B parameters, we demonstrate that BAS achieves performance on par with AdamW.
